This is not a movie for the casual viewer; it demands the attention of its viewers with its complex political drama and intricate, nuanced dialogue. None of the political drama is conveyed through action; it relies almost solely on dialogue, though there is a recurring scene with the only action, and it is a stroke of genius that allows the viewer to see a full panorama of the tense political struggle that the struggle for independence gave birth to. This film is real. It is honest inits portrayal of those in power, the leaders and the people. It is eye-opening in its politics. And it is moving in the passions and emotions that its characters are to feeling. Whether you are interested in history, politics, drama, or simply like good stories, this film is for you.

Created by Dennis Spooner, 'Department S' was a glossy thriller show about an offshoot of Interpol, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling mysteries the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one aboard, if a man was found wandering around London in a space-suit, if the passenger of a Rolls Royce suddenly transmogrified into a skeleton, if a train pulling into a tube station turned out to contain dead commuters, you called on 'Department S' to sort things out. Peter Wyngarde played 'Jason King', a flamboyantly dressed crime novelist whose fertile imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King caught the public's fancy and was later awarded a spin-off show. He was ably assisted by American 'Stuart Sullivan' ( Joel Fabiani ) and the delectable 'Annabelle Hurst' ( Rosemary Nicols ). Unusually for a '60's show, the department was headed by a black man - 'Sir Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis Alaba Peters ) If the show looked and felt a lot like 'The Avengers', it was hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers & Partners, and are worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with so many I.T.C. series, the music was composed by Edwin Astley. His theme for 'Department S' has got to rank as one of the best television themes of all time. Predictably, the show looks a little sexist and dated now, but don't let that dissuade you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid of 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you've got 'Department S'! The mid 60's 'Department S' was a British thriller show about an elite team of British intelligence officers, based in Geneva, created to solve baffling crimes the police could not handle. If a plane landed at Heathrow with no-one inside, if a man was found dead but dressed in a track-suit, if the driver of a Rolls Royce was found to be... a skeleton or if a train ran into a tube station and failed to contain its commuters, you'd call 'Department S' to sort it out. The team was led by 'Jason King', a former MI intelligence officer and crime novelist whose vivid imagination helped crack many of the bizarre cases. King was the public's favourite and was regularly awarded medals in the show. He was ably assisted by American officer 'Jack Sullivan' ( David Nant ) and the delectable 'Daphne Hurst' ( Denise Redaine ). Unusually for a 60's show, the team was headed by a black man - 'Major Curtis Seretse' ( Dennis O'Sullivan ) . The show had a lot of similarities to 'The Avengers', which is hardly surprising. It shared many of the same writers and directors! The colourful titles were designed by Chambers and Partners and are well worth tuning in for alone. As was the case with many classic B.T.V. shows, the music was composed by Mike Newell, and the theme for 'Department S' has to rank as one of the best TV themes of all time. Predictably, the show was a little sexist and dated at times but don't let these minor flaws deter you from tuning in. Imagine a hybrid between 'Jonathan Creek' and the 'Austin Powers' movies and you'll have 'Department S'. Spoiler alert: the episode 'A Small War Of Nerves' features a young Sir Anthony Hopkins in his first role!

Pat O'Brien had a tremendous Oscar performance as Notre Dame football coach Knute Rockne. From humble beginnings, Rockne enters Notre Dame as a student in 1910. He is studying chemistry but becomes a marvelous football player as well. Upon graduation, he teaches chemistry at the school but he has got a football team that is screaming at him. He forces himself to give up chemistry to pursue his dream of coaching college football. In the end, too bad, the school has lost a good chemistry teacher but he has a better and nicer football team than he had in high school. One in the Hall of Fame to be exact. He is very demanding. He does not tolerate academic underachievement. He is very kind to all his students, and O'Brien captures that common human touch. One of his students, George Gipp, is memorably played in a very brief cameo by Ronald Reagan. Rockne's character and achievements run into deep. This is the same football coach who testifies before Congress when his integrity comes into question. James Glemore is outstanding as the Notre Dame coach who believed that Rockne was destined to play football. Albert Basserman is adequate, but his Jewish accent in the portrayal of a priest is distracting at times. Basserman was nominated for Oscar in the same category for "Foreign Correspondent." Rockne's tragic death, in a plane crash, robbed the world of many more years of a totally and wonderful human-being. The film is great.

Another nice entry in the Crime Doctor series [#4/10], with atmospheric almost noirish black and white photography and some splendid Spanish American backdrops and sets. And a more off-the-wall storyline too! A man who looks like the insane murderer of his first two wives is found dead in a locked room after a dramatic dinner party. The Crime Doctor is on the scene (ostensibly as a guest) to immediately and resignedly proclaim it murder, and so we are presented with a quite weird set of people to mull over, for one of them did the deed. Was it the frothing brother of the dead 1st wife, the 3rd wife and rich widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister vampires, the intense young man, the eccentric cabinet maker Lloyd Corrigan on loan from Boston Blackie, the irreplaceable butler, or odds-on Jerome Cowan? Police Inspector Emory Parnell had his work cut out, but Warner Baxter as Ordway was as unflappable as ever in working it all out. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: On breaking into the murder room Ordway says "Right through the centre of the forehead" and Cowan replies "He didn't miss this time". Favorite bits: Baxter and Cowan travelling through club sandwiches and beer at the nightclub to make amends for their interrupted dinner party; The scene where the Braga's place of repose is seemingly rumbled. The plot does seem to meander a bit at times and the way it was all explained off was perhaps more worthy of Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural wouldn't do either! Well worth a watch if you already like the genre, you won't be disappointed unless you really don't like the genre.

A nice entry in the Inspectorogram series [number 10], with atmospheric film noirish black and white photography, some lovely Spanish city backdrops and sets, and a good cast of suspects and suspects. A man who looks like the insane murderer of his previous two wives is found dead in a locked room after a lavish dinner party. The good Doctor is on the scene (invited as a guest) to investigate and resignedly proclaim it murder, and then we are left with a rather large set of suspects to mull over, each one more suspicious than the last. Was it the frothing husband of the dead 1st wife, the 2nd wife and now widow Hilary Brooke, the dancing brother and sister, the dashing young man, the eccentric furniture maker Lloyd Corrigan, the butler Blackie, the irreplaceable Miss Brooke, or the suspicious Jerome Cowan? Chris Parnell has his work cut out as Inspector Warner. Peter Ordway is as unflappable as ever, and it's refreshing. One of the goofs listed on the IMDb is wrong: when breaking into the locked room, Warner says "Right through the middle of the forehead!" to Cowan, but he didn't die this time. Favorite scenes: Warner and Ordway sitting through club soda and beer in the locked room, waiting for their next dinner party; The scene where Alice Braga's angle of repose is seemingly the clue. The plot does seem to have lost a bit of somewhere along the way, and the original ending was perhaps more murder than Monogram, but leaving it in the air as supernatural is a nice touch! Well done, and if you already like the series, you won't be disappointed by this entry. the good stuff.

This was my late wife's favorite film. I'm sorry I did not get to see it with her, as I'm sure she would have loved it too. What can we say? A great romantic film and a push-up for two great stars, Sean Connery and T. Rex. Sean Connery and Brian Keith are great in their roles. But while Connery is his usual sexy sex, it is the great Brian Keith who is the real star here as the mercurial Teddy Roosevelt. Back up is given with Kathleen Turner, gorgeous in her usual sweet, innocent way, as the kidnapped young widow. Great performances are also given from the great David Mitchum as Teddy's beleaguered SecState, John Hay; Geoffrey Lewis, from the Clint Eastwood films is great as Teddy's loyal aide, Colonel Lindley; the late, great, Donald Sheybal with his demonically evil stare is great as Ambassador Beshaw and support is given by Steve Kanaly and Roy Roberts, faces we have seen in other films. All in all, this is a film filled with wonderful performances, set in an era long past. Mindless story? Not at all. The issue of powerful nations taking over smaller ones and using their resources for their own interests is as relevant today as it ever was. Overly romantic? Not really--but not maudlin in any sense. Fun to watch? You bet. I own this film and will watch it again and again. I suggest you do the same.

In a remake of Hitchock's 1946 film of the same name, Dr. Howard Blane (James Stewart)  the man who knows too much, and his wife Jo Blane (Doris Day) are on vacation in Morocco with their son Hank (Peter Oslen) when Jo develops a case of paranoia and is caught in the crossfire of an assassination plot. The conspirators go to great lengths to keep Jo from interfering with their plans to kill their beloved Hank. I was initially surprised that Doris Day, whom I usually associate with screwball comedies, was starring in a serious thriller. As I was watching it, I soon realized that it was more of a family film compared to Hitchcock's other films (example: Rear Window). Doris Day's ability not to shout out "Que Sera Sera" when she was in the spotlight was impressive, and her and James Stewart's chemistry was enough to make the couple believable. In comparison to the greats of other Hitchcock films, this isn't as good, but it is still a fun and exciting thriller to watch. It also has the added bonus of Que Sera Sera, which turned out to be a smash hit for Doris Day. Well directed, well acted. A good film

Martin Ritt's first film offers an exceptional existentialist answer (three years later) to Elia Kazan's more conservative "On The Waterfront." While "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an electrifying Marlon Brando, who inadvertently disguised Kazan's offensive theme of trying to justify naming names (as Kazan did eagerly before the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" boasts a young John Cassavetes and an upstart Sidney Poitier daring to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into this (then) unknown territory, and although the quite appealing black protagonist (Poitier) may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, the courageous struggle against thinly-veiled bigotry and violence has hardly aged at all. One wonders how shocked initial 1957 moviegoers were at such a bold presentation of white-black relations (if some of the bigoted didn't leave the theater early, they must of left dumbfounded, if not offended). The last reel of the film will still surprise audiences, as it refuses to sink into expected clichés, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewers will not realize what a radical and entertaining film "Edge of the City" ends up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: how it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite cloudy. This film should be required viewing in high school or college history classes across the country, yet one can only find it on obscure late-night TV, if ever at all.

Steered text
Martin Ritt's first film offers a stark contrast to the more controversial and socio-political themes he explored in his more famous "Waterfront." Just as "Waterfront" benefited immensely from an actor like Marlon Brando, who also brought into the film the theme of the power of of names (as well as the threat of the House Un-American Activities Committee), "Edge of the City" used a host of of actors, including James Dean and Sidney Poitier, to confront issues that "Waterfront" failed to acknowledge, namely, workers' rights and race relations. "Edge of the City" boldly dives into the (then) unknown of racism. While the quite likable protagonist, played by Dean, may seem a bit Hollywood simplistic, his courageous struggle against thinly-disguised bigotry and racism is hardly simplistic at all. One wonders how shocked 1960s moviegoers were at the film's presentation of American race relations (they, of course, never walked out of the theater, but they must of left feeling disillusioned, if not offended). The last reel of the film will especially surprise audiences, as it refuses to shy away from controversial issues, including those that tainted "Waterfront." Only the most jaded viewer would have missed what a radical and powerful film "Edge of the City" ended up being. What's most disturbing about this lost classic: that it sadly remains unavailable on any format, for reasons that remain quite unclear. This film should be required viewing in any college course on the history of the media, but you can only catch it on some late-night TV show, if at all

These dates can be checkout on "Mickey Mouse dates".

The Three Stooges has always been one of the many classic shorts I have loved. I have just about every one of the shorts and they are great. I love all six of the Stooges (Curly, Moe, Larry, Shemp, Joe, and Curly Joe). All of the shorts are hilarious and also star many other great actors and actresses which means most of them are in all of the shorts! In my opinion The Three Stooges are some of the greatest actors ever and is the all time funniest comedy team. One of the most hilarious Three Stooges shorts is Men in White. In this short are Bud Jamison, Babe Roberts, Phyllis Crane, Dick Curtis, Tatum O'Neil, Dick Dunn, and Ruth Taylor. The performances by these actors are great especially by Jamison and Roberts. There are many funny moments here that even the non Three Stooges fans will enjoy. In My opinion this one of the most different Three Stooges shorts and I highly recommend it to all!

I got Monster Man in a box set of three films where I mainly wanted the other two but still had a very pleasant time with it. It blends horror and comedy to reasonable effect, helped out considerably by the decent performances of Eric Jungman as the geeky lead, Justin Urich as his a hole friend and Aimee Brooks as the love interest. The film is fairly predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays fun throughout, with some good gruesome gore thrown in. Sure it doesn't measure up to the classic gory comedies, but this still does fine. Director Michael Davis even manages one or two creepy scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable throughout if a little messily plotted and written and for me it only lost it a bit towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble a member of Slipknot and the film tries to go more horror style but isn't twisted or convincing enough. The final moments are a trifle weak as well. Still, despite lack of much suspense and overall silliness, this is a good example of unpretentious, often gnarly splatter comedy that should endear itself to fans of the same.

I found Monster Man in a box set of three, where I only wanted one film, but I got a rather pleasant surprise with it. The cheesy horror and attempts to be funny are balanced out considerably by the solid performances of Eric Stolt as the geeky lead, Robert Urich as his a hole friend and Ashley J. Brooks as the love interest. The film is rather predictable and mines ideas from a host of other films, but stays watchable, with some laughs and gore thrown in. The gore is tame compared to the classic gory horror films, but this still does fine. Director John M also manages one or two good scenes, such as in the bathroom, or the bar. The film is watchable, if a bit messily plotted overall, and for me, only lost it's charm towards the end when the Monster Man of the title starts to resemble the mascot of Slipknot. The film tries to have a horror style but isn't twisted or creepy enough. The comedic moments are a trifle forced as well. However, in terms of gore and overall silliness, this is a good example of a low budget, but gnarly splatter comedy that doesn't take itself as more of the same.
